name: Dissociation battery: the unit's sensitivity across a fixed library of control transforms
compute: Build one library of about 30–60 transforms. Each transform is chosen to disrupt one candidate property while sparing the others. Examples: translation, which changes position but keeps chirality; 180° rotation versus horizontal flip versus vertical flip; small versus large rotation angles; hue rotation, saturation-only and luminance-only changes, and colour-histogram matching; phase scrambling, which keeps the amplitude spectrum, versus amplitude whitening, which keeps phase; low-pass and high-pass filtering; patch shuffles at grid sizes 2, 4, 8 and 16; local pixel shuffles; texture-preserving and shape-preserving synthesis; contrast inversion; crop and rescale. For every unit and every transform, compute a normalised sensitivity: 1 − corr(a(x), a(t(x))) over the image set, or the mean |Δa| divided by the unit's activation SD. Then express each value as a z-score against the same layer's units. This gives each unit a sensitivity vector. Also tag each transform with the properties it disrupts, as a binary matrix written by hand once, and fit sensitivity ≈ Σ property weights using non-negative least squares.
show: A ranked bar chart of the unit's z-scored sensitivity to every transform, with T highlighted. Pair it with the property-tag matrix and the fitted property weights. Add the 3 transforms whose effect on the unit is closest to T's and the 3 that are most similar to T in pixel terms but spare the unit, for example 'flip hurts, translate does not, 180° rotation does not'.
read: The property responsible is the one shared by the transforms that disrupt the unit and missing from the look-alike transforms that spare it. Example: flip hurts, 180° rotation and translation do not. This points to chirality or text-like handedness, not position. Another example: a patch shuffle hurts only at fine grids and phase scrambling also hurts. This points to local shape or edge configuration, not global layout. If no single property explains the pattern (poor fit, or several large weights), report a conjunction or 'unresolved' rather than forcing one name.
cost: No labels. You hand-write the transform property tags once and reuse them for every model. Compute is |library| forward passes over N images, shared across every unit in the layer, so it is cheap: one batched pass per transform.
text: A library of text transforms: token shuffles within a window of k for several k; sentence-order shuffles; shuffles across sentences versus within them; reversal; a pure position shift made by prepending neutral padding (the translation analogue); case changes; whitespace or tokenisation re-segmentation that keeps the characters; typos; synonym swaps; paraphrases; translation into another language; replacing entity names; negation insertion; removing punctuation or numbers; replacing content words with others of the same part of speech. Tag the properties each transform disrupts (lexical identity, local order, syntax, discourse order, absolute position, surface form, semantics) and fit the same way.

name: Equivariance check: is the feature destroyed or merely moved?
compute: For transforms with a known spatial mapping (flips, rotations, translations, patch shuffles with a known permutation), compare a(T(x)) with T applied to the unit's spatial activation map, T(a(x)). Separate the total drop into three parts. The first is a moved component: the response follows the content to its new place, which matters when the profile read a fixed location or used asymmetric pooling. The second is a destroyed component: the response disappears even after re-alignment. The third is a boundary component: the change comes from content crossing the edge of the receptive field or the padding. Also compute the spatially max-pooled sensitivity next to the fixed-location sensitivity.
show: For 6–8 images: the original image, the transformed image, a(x), a(T(x)) and the re-aligned T(a(x)), all on a shared colour scale. Add one summary number for each component (moved, destroyed, boundary) and the pooled-versus-located sensitivity.
read: If most of the sensitivity is 'moved', the unit is not sensitive to the property T seems to target (for example orientation). It is selective for position or location, or the profile is an artefact of how it was read out. Only the 'destroyed' component is evidence about content. If the boundary component is large, the cause is padding or edge effects, not image content. Run this before interpreting any other test.
cost: No labels. Compute is the forward passes already done for test 1, plus storing spatial maps and applying a known inverse mapping. Transforms without a spatial mapping, such as colour or blur, need no re-alignment, so the step is trivial for them.
text: Align token positions under T (permutation for shuffles, offset for prepended padding, character-span alignment for re-tokenisation). Compare the unit's activation at token i in x with its activation at the aligned token in T(x). Separate 'the feature moved with its token' from 'the token kept its feature but lost it' (context-dependent) and from 'position or absolute-index effect' (the padding shift). Show the two sequences with per-token activations aligned.

name: Graded and localised T: dose-response and scope restriction
compute: (a) Dose: sweep T's strength (angle, blur σ, shuffle grid size or fraction of patches moved, hue shift in degrees, interpolation α between x and T(x)) and record the unit's mean response curve. (b) Scope: apply T only inside the unit's effective receptive field, or only inside its top-attribution region, versus only outside it. Use soft masks so no new edges are created. (c) Where T is composite, split it into components: colour change into hue, saturation and luminance; rotation into crop-free and padded versions. Normalise everything by the size of the image-level change, such as LPIPS or pixel L2, so that 'sensitive' is not just 'T changes a lot of pixels'.
show: Response-versus-strength curves for the unit, with the layer's median unit as a reference band. A 2×2 table of inside versus outside the receptive field against T on versus off. A per-component bar chart for composite transforms.
read: A threshold or step at a particular grid size or angle gives the spatial scale of the property. For example, a drop only when the patch size falls below the object-part size means the unit needs part-level configuration. A smooth linear drop with blur suggests reliance on a frequency band, not a discrete feature. If the drop happens only when T is applied inside the receptive field, the property is local. If T outside the receptive field matters, the unit encodes context or a global statistic such as overall colour cast or scene layout. A clear win for one component isolates it.
cost: No labels. Compute is about 5–10 strengths × 3 scopes × N images per transform. The receptive field comes from one gradient pass per image. Moderate cost, but it only needs to run for T and for the top transforms from test 1.
text: Dose: shuffle window size, fraction of tokens perturbed, number of typos, distance of the swapped spans. Scope: apply T only to the tokens that attribution shows drive the unit at the readout position, versus only to distant context, versus only to tokens after the readout (these should have no effect under causal attention, which makes it a sanity check). Split composite transforms, for example paraphrase into lexical substitution versus reordering.

name: Most and least affected examples with an automatic concept correlation
compute: For every image, compute Δ = a(x) − a(T(x)) at the unit's peak location after alignment as in test 2. Rank the images. Compare the top-k most affected with images that have similarly high a(x) but small Δ; matching on a(x) controls for the fact that only strongly activating images can drop a lot. Run a concept scorer over the images (zero-shot CLIP or VLM scores for a fixed vocabulary of about 500 concepts, plus cheap statistics such as presence of text or faces, symmetry, dominant hue, edge density, horizon tilt, centre of mass) and correlate each concept with Δ, holding a(x) fixed. If the dataset has class labels, also break Δ down by class.
show: A grid of the 12 most affected pairs (x and T(x), with heatmaps of a(x) and a(T(x))) next to 12 matched pairs that spared the unit. List the top 10 concepts by partial correlation with Δ, with effect sizes and a shuffled-label null. Add a short per-class Δ table if labels exist.
read: Look for what the affected images share that the spared images, matched on activation, lack. Example: all flip-affected images contain written text or a left-facing object. That means handedness of a specific content, not a generic property. Accept a concept only if it is visible in the exemplars and also significant above the null. If the drop is spread evenly across all high-activation images, the property is intrinsic to what the unit detects, not to a subset of content.
cost: Optional labels: class labels if available. The concept vocabulary is fixed once. Compute is one CLIP or VLM pass per image, shared across units, plus the Δ values that already exist. Low marginal cost per unit.
text: Rank sequences or tokens by Δ, matched on base activation. Show the most and least affected snippets with per-token activation highlighting before and after T. Correlate Δ with automatic tags: part of speech, dependency depth, named entities, language, code versus prose, quotations, numbers, token frequency, and position in the document. A tagger or LLM annotator supplies the tags.

name: Mediation by upstream units: which inputs carry the change
compute: Measure how much of the unit's Δ under T passes through each upstream unit or channel. Use activation patching: take the run on T(x) and restore individual upstream channels (or channel groups or spatial blocks) to their values from the clean run on x. Record how much of the drop each restoration recovers. Alternatively use the first-order estimate Δupstream × gradient. Keep the top mediators and attach whatever labels they already have: the result of this pipeline run on them earlier, or their top-activating exemplars. Do the same at the input level by restoring individual colour channels, frequency bands or spatial patches of x into T(x).
show: The 5 upstream channels or input bands that recover the most of the drop, each with the fraction recovered, its own top exemplars or existing label, and its own sensitivity to T. Also a map of which input patches or bands, when restored, bring the response back.
read: If restoring one or two upstream channels brings the response back, T matters because it disrupts what those channels detect, so their known property (for example 'oriented red–green edges') is the explanation. If the recovery is spread over many channels, the unit depends on how features are configured together, not on one input feature. Combine with test 1: the mediators should be sensitive to the same transforms that disrupt the unit.
cost: No labels, though it benefits from earlier interpretations of upstream units. Compute is the highest of the five, about one forward pass per patched group per image. Use the gradient approximation, a subset of about 200 images, and grouped channels to keep it cheap.
text: Patch residual-stream components (attention heads, MLP outputs, SAE features of earlier layers) from the clean run on x into the run on T(x) at the readout position and at the source tokens. Report which heads or features recover the unit's activation, along with their attention patterns before and after T. Example: a previous-token head whose source is lost under a shuffle points to local order. Do the same at the input by restoring individual token embeddings or spans.
